items.title: A client with a tibial fracture reports escalating pain despite opioid analgesia. The affected foot is tense and pain increases with passive toe movement. What should the nurse do?
items.content: Notify the orthopedic team immediately and prepare for urgent evaluation.
items.rationale: Pain out of proportion and pain with passive stretch are early signs of compartment syndrome. Delay can cause irreversible neurovascular injury.

items.title: A client receiving chemotherapy has an oral temperature of 38.4 °C (101.1 °F) and an absolute neutrophil count of 300/mm³. What is the priority?
items.content: Initiate the febrile-neutropenia protocol and notify the oncology team immediately.
items.rationale: Fever with profound neutropenia is an oncologic emergency. Cultures and prompt empiric broad-spectrum antimicrobials are time-sensitive.

items.title: A client with myasthenia gravis develops a weak cough, difficulty swallowing, and declining vital capacity. What is the priority concern?
items.content: Impending respiratory failure requiring urgent airway and ventilatory assessment.
items.rationale: Bulbar weakness and declining respiratory capacity can progress rapidly to respiratory failure. Escalate before exhaustion or arrest.

items.title: A client with known adrenal insufficiency has vomiting, severe weakness, BP 78/42 mm Hg, sodium 126 mEq/L, and potassium 5.9 mEq/L. Which treatment should the nurse anticipate?
items.content: Urgent IV hydrocortisone and isotonic fluid resuscitation as prescribed.
items.rationale: Adrenal crisis causes cortisol deficiency, hypotension, hyponatremia, and often hyperkalemia. Steroid replacement and volume resuscitation are urgent.

items.title: During a rapid vancomycin infusion, a client develops flushing and pruritus over the face and upper torso. What should the nurse do?
items.content: Stop or slow the infusion per protocol, assess the client, and notify the prescriber.
items.rationale: An infusion-related reaction is associated with rapid administration. Assess for airway compromise and hypotension; future doses may require slower infusion and prescribed premedication.

items.title: A prescription reads potassium chloride 10 mEq IV push for a client with hypokalemia. What should the nurse do?
items.content: Do not administer; clarify the prescription because IV potassium must never be given by IV push.
items.rationale: Concentrated potassium given by IV push can cause fatal dysrhythmias. It must be diluted and infused at a controlled rate with appropriate monitoring.

items.title: A pregnant client at 32 weeks has painless bright-red vaginal bleeding. Which assessment should the nurse avoid until placenta location is confirmed?
items.content: Digital vaginal examination.
items.rationale: Placenta previa can cause catastrophic hemorrhage with cervical manipulation. Avoid digital examination until ultrasound excludes previa.

items.title: During labor, a client suddenly develops severe dyspnea, cyanosis, hypotension, and bleeding from IV sites. What should the team suspect?
items.content: Amniotic fluid embolism with cardiopulmonary collapse and coagulopathy.
items.rationale: Sudden hypoxia, cardiovascular collapse, and disseminated coagulopathy during labor or shortly after birth are characteristic warning features. Activate emergency multidisciplinary response.

items.title: A 9-month-old has episodic severe crying with knees drawn to the chest, vomiting, and currant-jelly stool. Which condition should the nurse suspect?
items.content: Intussusception.
items.rationale: Intermittent colicky pain, vomiting, and bloody mucus stool are classic findings. Prompt evaluation is needed because bowel ischemia or perforation can occur.

items.title: A 3-year-old has fever for 6 days, bilateral nonpurulent conjunctival injection, cracked lips, and swollen hands. Which complication is most important to prevent?
items.content: Coronary artery aneurysm.
items.rationale: Kawasaki disease causes vasculitis with risk of coronary artery involvement. Timely IV immunoglobulin and aspirin therapy are used under specialist direction.

items.title: A client 18 hours after the last drink develops tremors, diaphoresis, tachycardia, and agitation. Which intervention should the nurse anticipate?
items.content: Administer prescribed benzodiazepine using the withdrawal protocol and monitor closely.
items.rationale: Benzodiazepines reduce withdrawal severity and seizure risk. Monitor autonomic instability, mental status, hydration, and progression to delirium tremens.

items.title: A client with suspected infectious pulmonary tuberculosis must leave the room for imaging. What protection should the nurse ensure for transport?
items.content: The client wears a surgical mask during transport; staff use fit-tested respiratory protection as indicated.
items.rationale: The patient wears a surgical mask to reduce droplet nuclei dispersal during transport. Staff entering the airborne isolation room require an appropriate fit-tested respirator.

items.title: A client after cardiac surgery has hypotension, jugular venous distention, muffled heart sounds, and narrowing pulse pressure. What complication should the nurse suspect?
items.content: Cardiac tamponade.
items.rationale: Beck triad and hemodynamic compromise suggest tamponade, which restricts ventricular filling. This requires immediate escalation and likely urgent drainage.

items.title: A client found after prolonged immobilization has muscle pain, dark urine, and markedly elevated creatine kinase. Which actions should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Administer prescribed isotonic IV fluids; monitor potassium and renal function; measure urine output; assess for dysrhythmias.
items.rationale: Rhabdomyolysis releases myoglobin and potassium, risking acute kidney injury and hyperkalemia. Early fluids and close renal/electrolyte monitoring are central.

items.title: A client is admitted with suspected meningococcal meningitis. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Initiate droplet precautions; administer prescribed antimicrobials promptly; monitor neurologic status; assess for signs of increased intracranial pressure.
items.rationale: Meningococcal disease requires droplet precautions until appropriate treatment duration. Prompt antimicrobials and neurologic monitoring reduce morbidity and detect complications.

items.title: A client will take prednisone for several weeks. Which teaching points are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Take with food; do not stop prolonged therapy abruptly; report fever or signs of infection; monitor glucose as directed.
items.rationale: Corticosteroids can cause gastrointestinal irritation, immunosuppression, hyperglycemia, and adrenal suppression. Tapering may be required after prolonged use.

items.title: A client with severe preeclampsia is receiving magnesium sulfate. Which findings require immediate action? Select all that apply.
items.content: Respiratory rate 9/min; absent deep tendon reflexes; urine output 20 mL over 2 hours.
items.rationale: Respiratory depression, absent reflexes, and oliguria suggest magnesium accumulation and toxicity. Stop the infusion, escalate, support breathing, and prepare prescribed calcium gluconate.

items.title: A toddler has barking cough and inspiratory stridor at rest. Which interventions should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Keep the child calm; administer prescribed dexamethasone; administer nebulized epinephrine for significant stridor; reassess for rebound symptoms.
items.rationale: Corticosteroids reduce airway inflammation. Nebulized epinephrine provides temporary relief in moderate-to-severe croup; observe after treatment for recurrence.

items.title: A client experiencing a panic attack is hyperventilating and says, “I am going to die.” Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Stay with the client; use short, calm statements; reduce environmental stimulation; coach slow breathing when the client can engage.
items.rationale: Presence and calm, simple communication reduce fear and stimulation. Avoid complex teaching during peak panic; assess for medical causes when indicated.

items.title: A client with recurrent seizures is admitted to the unit. Which safety measures are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.content: Pad side rails per policy; keep suction and oxygen available; maintain a low bed; during a seizure protect the head and turn the client laterally when possible.
items.rationale: Environmental preparation reduces injury and supports airway management. Do not restrain the client or place objects in the mouth during a seizure.

items.title: A client with acute liver failure is confused and has asterixis, rising INR, and hypoglycemia. Select the 3 complications that require close monitoring.
items.content: Encephalopathy progression; bleeding; recurrent hypoglycemia.
items.rationale: Hepatic failure impairs ammonia clearance, clotting factor synthesis, and glucose regulation. Neurologic status, bleeding, and glucose require close monitoring.

items.title: A client with type 1 diabetes using an insulin pump has nausea, glucose 380 mg/dL, and positive blood ketones. Select the 3 immediate actions.
items.content: Check the infusion set and pump for interruption; check electrolytes and acid-base status; initiate the prescribed DKA evaluation and treatment pathway.
items.rationale: Pump users receive only rapid-acting insulin, so interruption can quickly cause ketosis. Evaluate for DKA and restore insulin delivery according to clinical orders.

items.title: A newborn of a diabetic parent is jittery and feeds poorly. Select the 3 priority actions.
items.content: Check bedside blood glucose promptly; assess temperature and respiratory status; initiate prescribed feeding or dextrose treatment based on the result and symptoms.
items.rationale: Jitteriness and poor feeding may indicate neonatal hypoglycemia. Rapid glucose measurement and protocol-based treatment prevent neurologic injury.

items.title: A client with a casted lower leg reports worsening pain. Select the 3 findings most concerning for compartment syndrome.
items.content: Pain unrelieved by analgesia; pain with passive stretch; tense swelling of the compartment.
items.rationale: These are early warning signs of rising compartment pressure. Paresthesia and paralysis are later findings; urgent surgical evaluation is required.

items.title: Match each presentation with the most likely shock type.
items.content: rows:massive gastrointestinal bleeding with cool clammy skin;acute myocardial infarction with pulmonary edema and hypotension;spinal cord injury with hypotension and bradycardia|columns:hypovolemic;cardiogenic;neurogenic|answers:massive gastrointestinal bleeding with cool clammy skin=hypovolemic;acute myocardial infarction with pulmonary edema and hypotension=cardiogenic;spinal cord injury with hypotension and bradycardia=neurogenic
items.rationale: Hemorrhage causes loss of circulating volume. Pump failure after MI causes cardiogenic shock. Loss of sympathetic tone after spinal injury can produce neurogenic shock with bradycardia.

items.title: Match each toxic exposure with its antidote.
items.content: rows:opioid toxicity;acetaminophen overdose;heparin-associated bleeding|columns:naloxone;N-acetylcysteine;protamine sulfate|answers:opioid toxicity=naloxone;acetaminophen overdose=N-acetylcysteine;heparin-associated bleeding=protamine sulfate
items.rationale: Naloxone reverses opioid effects. N-acetylcysteine limits acetaminophen-related hepatic injury. Protamine reverses unfractionated heparin.

items.title: For each stroke-related finding, select all appropriate nursing actions.
items.content: rows:suspected acute stroke before imaging;dysphagia after stroke;new decline in consciousness|columns:establish last-known-well time;keep NPO until swallow screen;activate urgent neurologic reassessment;give oral fluids to test swallowing|answers:suspected acute stroke before imaging=establish last-known-well time,activate urgent neurologic reassessment;dysphagia after stroke=keep NPO until swallow screen;new decline in consciousness=activate urgent neurologic reassessment
items.rationale: Time of onset guides treatment eligibility. Swallow screening is required before oral intake to reduce aspiration. A new neurologic decline requires immediate reassessment and escalation.

items.title: For each risk or finding, select all appropriate preventive responses.
items.content: rows:urinary incontinence;limited mobility;nonblanchable sacral erythema|columns:cleanse and apply moisture barrier;individualized repositioning and heel offloading;pressure redistribution and skin assessment;massage reddened bony prominence|answers:urinary incontinence=cleanse and apply moisture barrier;limited mobility=individualized repositioning and heel offloading,pressure redistribution and skin assessment;nonblanchable sacral erythema=pressure redistribution and skin assessment,individualized repositioning and heel offloading
items.rationale: Moisture management and pressure redistribution reduce tissue injury. Nonblanchable erythema requires offloading and assessment; massage can worsen damaged tissue.

items.title: A client with a positive pregnancy test has unilateral pelvic pain, shoulder-tip pain, and hypotension. Suspect a ruptured ___. Prioritize assessment for ___ and prepare for urgent ___.
items.content: ectopic pregnancy|hemorrhagic shock|surgical management
items.rationale: Unilateral pain, referred shoulder pain, and hypotension suggest intra-abdominal bleeding from ruptured ectopic pregnancy. Stabilization and urgent surgical management are required.

items.title: An older adult with glucose 920 mg/dL, profound dehydration, and altered mentation may have ___. Initial management includes prescribed ___ fluids and close monitoring of serum ___.
items.content: hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state|isotonic|osmolality and electrolytes
items.rationale: HHS causes profound hyperglycemia and hyperosmolality with dehydration. Isotonic fluid resuscitation is initiated, with careful monitoring of sodium, potassium, osmolality, and neurologic status.

items.title: Minutes after receiving an antibiotic, a client develops generalized urticaria, wheezing, lip swelling, and BP 76/40 mm Hg. Select the condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:anaphylaxis|actions:administer IM epinephrine promptly as prescribed or protocol-directed;support airway and oxygenation and activate emergency response|monitor:airway patency and respiratory effort;blood pressure and perfusion
items.rationale: Rapid multisystem symptoms with hypotension after exposure indicate anaphylaxis. IM epinephrine is first-line; airway support and hemodynamic monitoring are essential.

items.title: A 13-year-old with type 1 diabetes has abdominal pain, Kussmaul respirations, glucose 480 mg/dL, pH 7.12, and positive ketones. Select the condition, two actions, and two parameters to monitor.
items.content: condition:diabetic ketoacidosis|actions:begin prescribed isotonic fluid resuscitation;initiate IV insulin after confirming potassium is safe|monitor:serum potassium and cardiac rhythm;neurologic status and glucose/ketone trend
items.rationale: The findings establish DKA with acidosis and dehydration. Fluids are initiated; insulin is started only after potassium assessment because insulin can worsen hypokalemia. Monitor electrolytes, rhythm, and neurologic status.

items.title: Highlight the findings in a client taking an SSRI who recently started linezolid that suggest serotonin syndrome: inducible clonus; hyperreflexia; temperature 39.1 °C; isolated dry skin; new agitation and diaphoresis.
items.content: segments:inducible clonus|hyperreflexia|temperature 39.1 C|isolated dry skin|new agitation and diaphoresis|correct:1,2,3,5
items.rationale: Clonus, hyperreflexia, hyperthermia, agitation, and diaphoresis after serotonergic drug interaction suggest serotonin syndrome. Stop serotonergic agents as directed and escalate urgently.

items.title: Highlight findings in a client with abdominal pain that require urgent surgical evaluation: rigid boardlike abdomen; rebound tenderness; mild hunger; sudden pain relief followed by hypotension; chronic unchanged constipation.
items.content: segments:rigid boardlike abdomen|rebound tenderness|mild hunger|sudden pain relief followed by hypotension|chronic unchanged constipation|correct:1,2,4
items.rationale: Rigidity and rebound suggest peritoneal irritation. Sudden pain relief followed by hypotension may indicate perforation with deterioration. Urgent surgical assessment is required.

items.title: A client weighs 72 kg and is 1.60 m tall. Calculate BMI to one decimal place.
items.rationale: BMI = weight ÷ height squared = 72 ÷ (1.60 × 1.60) = 28.125, rounded to 28.1 kg/m².

items.title: A medication diluted in 100 mL is prescribed to infuse over 30 minutes. What pump rate should be programmed in mL/hr?
items.rationale: 30 minutes is 0.5 hour. 100 mL ÷ 0.5 hour = 200 mL/hr. Verify drug-specific infusion limits and compatibility.

items.title: Arrange the initial nursing actions for a client with sudden unilateral weakness in priority order.
items.content: Activate the stroke response and note last-known-well time.|Assess airway, breathing, circulation, and bedside glucose.|Prepare for urgent noncontrast head CT and prescribed stroke evaluation.|Maintain NPO status until swallowing safety is assessed.
items.rationale: Stroke activation and time documentation preserve treatment options. Stabilization and glucose assessment identify immediate threats and mimics. CT distinguishes hemorrhage; NPO status reduces aspiration risk.

items.title: Arrange the immediate team response to shoulder dystocia.
items.content: Call for help and announce shoulder dystocia.|Assist the client into McRoberts position.|Apply suprapubic pressure as directed by the obstetric clinician.|Prepare for additional maneuvers and neonatal resuscitation support.
items.rationale: Shoulder dystocia requires rapid coordinated maneuvers. McRoberts positioning and suprapubic pressure are initial techniques; fundal pressure must not be used.

items.title: A hospitalized client has rising creatinine after contrast imaging. Select all appropriate nursing actions.
items.content: Review and report nephrotoxic medications; monitor urine output and creatinine; assess volume status and administer prescribed fluids; trend potassium and other electrolytes; restrict all fluids without an order.
items.rationale: Review nephrotoxins, monitor renal function and electrolytes, assess volume, and follow prescribed hydration. Unordered fluid restriction may worsen renal perfusion.

items.title: An older adult hospitalized with infection becomes intermittently disoriented at night. Select all appropriate nursing interventions.
items.content: Provide clocks and familiar orientation cues; promote sleep and daytime mobilization; ensure hearing aids and glasses are available; assess pain, oxygenation, hydration, and medication effects; use restraints routinely to prevent wandering.
items.rationale: Delirium care focuses on identifying reversible causes and nonpharmacologic support. Sensory aids, orientation, sleep, mobility, hydration, and pain control help; routine restraints can worsen agitation.

items.title: A client taking warfarin has INR values of 2.2 on Monday, 3.4 on Wednesday, and 5.8 on Friday, with new gum bleeding. What is the priority interpretation?
items.content: The client has excessive anticoagulation with active bleeding; hold further doses pending urgent prescriber direction and assess for additional bleeding.
items.rationale: A rising INR above the usual therapeutic range with bleeding indicates increased hemorrhage risk. Further dosing requires urgent prescriber review and individualized reversal decisions.

items.title: A postpartum client's fundus changes from firm to boggy; lochia increases from scant to heavy with clots; HR rises from 82 to 126/min and BP falls from 118/74 to 88/52 mm Hg. What is the priority?
items.content: Recognize postpartum hemorrhage and initiate immediate hemorrhage response.
items.rationale: The combination of uterine atony, heavy bleeding, tachycardia, and hypotension indicates significant blood loss. Immediate escalation, uterine massage, quantified blood loss, uterotonics, and resuscitation are required.

items.title: A 5-year-old with fever and vomiting is lethargic. HR 158/min, RR 34/min, BP 78/42 mm Hg, capillary refill 5 seconds, cool extremities, and urine output 0.3 mL/kg/hr. Which condition is most likely and what are the immediate priorities?
items.content: Suspect septic shock. Activate the pediatric sepsis pathway, obtain cultures if this does not delay antimicrobials, administer prescribed isotonic fluid boluses with frequent reassessment, give prompt antimicrobials, and monitor perfusion and urine output.
items.rationale: Hypotension, delayed refill, cool extremities, oliguria, and altered mentation indicate shock. Pediatric resuscitation requires rapid protocol-based fluids and antimicrobials with reassessment for fluid responsiveness and overload.

items.title: An older adult taking digoxin and furosemide reports anorexia, nausea, and yellow halos. HR is 48/min and potassium is 2.9 mEq/L; creatinine has increased from baseline. What is the priority nursing response?
items.content: Withhold digoxin, notify the prescriber urgently, obtain ECG and ordered digoxin/electrolyte/renal studies, and monitor for dysrhythmias.
items.rationale: Bradycardia, visual changes, gastrointestinal symptoms, hypokalemia, and renal impairment strongly suggest digoxin toxicity. Hypokalemia and reduced clearance increase risk for serious dysrhythmias.
